title: Implement disaster recovery processes
summary: Disaster recovery processes turn an approved recovery strategy into coordinated preparation, emergency response, assessment, restoration, communications, and return-to-normal activities.
outcome: Given a disaster scenario, sequence the disaster-recovery process, identify the people and dependencies involved, preserve decision evidence, and coordinate recovery without treating restoration as the whole plan.
managerMindset: A DR plan is an executable coordination system for people, decisions, communications, technology, suppliers, and evidence under stress.

sections.title: Coordinate the process
sections.body: A disaster-recovery process commonly includes activation criteria, emergency response and life safety, notification, assessment, stabilization, recovery operations, data and system restoration, validation, business acceptance, and return to normal. Assign roles and alternates, maintain contact information and dependencies, protect plan access, and make decisions traceable. A recovery team should know what it may do immediately and what requires escalation.
keyPoints: Life safety and emergency communications precede technology restoration.
Activation criteria and authority should be explicit before a crisis.
Dependencies include people, facilities, power, communications, suppliers, data, identity, and keys.

sections.title: Restore, validate, and transition
sections.body: Recovery actions should use protected backups or alternate capabilities, verify system and data integrity, re-establish security controls, and monitor heightened risk. Business owners accept service against the recovery objectives and criteria; the team then manages backlog, communications, evidence, and return to normal or a sustained alternate mode. Record what worked, what failed, and which plan, contract, architecture, or training change is required.
keyPoints: A recovered system must be secure and usable, not merely powered on.
Business acceptance and security validation are distinct but coordinated decisions.
Return-to-normal can create another change and must be governed.

workedExamples.title: Regional data-center outage
workedExamples.situation: A flood closes a data center and interrupts power, access, network connectivity, and staff travel.
workedExamples.reasoning: Activate the plan based on impact and safety, establish communications and a decision log, assess dependencies and available alternate processing, protect evidence and personnel, recover critical services in priority order, validate identity and data controls, and obtain business acceptance. Treat return to the original site as a separate change and risk decision.

distinctions.difference: DR restores technology and dependent capabilities after disruption; BC keeps prioritized business functions operating and includes broader people, process, facility, supplier, and communication planning.
Emergency response protects life, safety, and immediate stabilization; recovery restores prioritized services and operations.

misconceptions.misconception: The DR coordinator can make every business-priority decision.
misconceptions.correction: Business owners, technical leads, security, facilities, communications, legal, and executives each provide authority and acceptance for their decisions.

misconceptions.misconception: A backup proves the service can be recovered.
misconceptions.correction: Recovery requires usable, trustworthy data, dependencies, access, keys, procedures, staff, capacity, and validation.

recallChecks.prompt: What comes before technology restoration in a disaster?
recallChecks.answer: Life safety, emergency response, notification, authority, and initial impact assessment.

recallChecks.prompt: What makes a recovered service acceptable?
recallChecks.answer: It meets agreed business and security criteria, has validated data and dependencies, and is accepted by the responsible owners.
Moving back changes systems, dependencies, access, and risk and can cause another outage if uncontrolled.

scenarioSeeds.scenario: The alternate site can run the application but has no current contact list for the identity, network, and key-management teams.
scenarioSeeds.decision: Treat contacts and dependencies as a recovery gap, activate alternates, and update and test the plan before relying on that site.
scenarioSeeds.why: Technical capacity without people and trust dependencies is not an executable DR capability.

studyPlan.learn: Study DR activation, emergency response, assessment, recovery teams, alternate sites, backups, communications, validation, and return to normal.

visualLearningContract.teachingQuestion: Who declares, restores, validates, accepts, and transitions DR service?
visualLearningContract.formRationale: Aligned columns make concept meanings, decision criteria and failure consequences explicit and comparable.
visualLearningContract.retrievalPrompt: Name objective, dependency, owner, evidence, acceptance.
visualLearningContract.textFallback:
Disaster Recovery Process: The accountable process for restoring mission-critical technology and its dependencies after a disaster, within approved business recovery objectives. Decision: Activate based on declared impact, recovery priorities, available strategy, authority, and safety conditions. Failure: Treating DR as only backup restoration misses people, communications, dependencies, validation, and business acceptance.
Emergency Response: Immediate actions that protect life, stabilize the event, preserve essential evidence, and enable a safe handoff to assessment and recovery. Decision: Prioritize life safety and incident stabilization before recovery acceleration; coordinate with authorized responders. Failure: Starting technical restoration while hazards or active compromise remain can harm people or destroy evidence.
Damage Assessment: The rapid assessment that determines affected scope, criticality, safety constraints, and feasible recovery options. Decision: Use current evidence to choose whether to recover in place, use an alternate capability, or escalate. Failure: Selecting a site or restore path before assessing dependencies can make the chosen plan impossible to execute.
Recovery Team: The assigned technical and business participants who execute recovery tasks and communicate status under designated authority. Decision: Select members and alternates for the services, facilities, suppliers, skills, and shifts actually in scope. Failure: A team with no business owner or dependency expertise may restore infrastructure without restoring the required service.
Alternate Site: A prearranged recovery location or capability selected to meet service objectives while avoiding the primary event’s correlated risks. Decision: Choose based on recovery-time/data objectives, capacity, geographic and utility separation, security controls, and test evidence. Failure: A nearby or untested site can share the same disaster impact or fail to support required capacity and security.
Backup Storage: Protected recovery copies and their storage service, managed for recoverability, integrity, access control, retention, and required recovery point. Decision: Select based on recovery-point objective, restoration time, geographic/administrative separation, immutability or protection needs, and proven restore process. Failure: A copy is not a recovery capability if it is inaccessible, corrupted, too old, compromised, or cannot be restored in time.
Return To Normal: A deliberate exit from recovery mode after validated service, reconciled data, accepted residual risk, communications, and documented closure. Decision: Transition when stable normal operations and all required acceptance evidence are available. Failure: Switching back solely because systems are up can reintroduce unresolved defects or abandon temporary safeguards.
Recovery Communications: Managed communications that provide accurate decisions, status, constraints, and instructions to each relevant audience throughout recovery. Decision: Use alternate channels, message ownership, approved facts, notification thresholds, and recorded decisions. Failure: Uncoordinated updates can cause unsafe actions, duplicated work, misinformation, or regulatory/customer harm.
